items.value: All three are correct: a mild surrender read as radical, limits distinguished from laziness, and 'leading man' repurposed from action to rest
items.reasoning: The passage calls the nap 'something quietly radical' and sets it against 'society's relentless performance metrics', so statement 1's link between a mild surrender and radicalism in the face of societal expectation is supported by the text. Statement 2 is near-verbatim: 'he made an elegant case for surrender. Not to laziness, but to limits', with age ('a 64-year-old man') named among the factors. Statement 3 restates the closing line, 'a leading man, not of action, but of rest', against the ordinary cinematic sense of the phrase. Runner-up is B (2 and 3 only), which wins if statement 1's generalisation from one nap to the principle that 'radical action can also be attributed to mild surrender' is judged an over-reach beyond what the passage licenses.

items.value: Only statement 3 is correct: Grant places the body's wisdom above the demands of society
items.reasoning: Statement 1 fails on a single word: the passage says he was watching 'the men's singles quarterfinals', not the semifinal. Statement 2 gets its first half right, since 'serving up an unexpected ace' does borrow a tennis term for the nap, but its closing claim that the act 'is viewed with opprobrium' is directly contradicted by 'So praise be to Grant'. Statement 3 restates 'the body's quiet wisdom over society's relentless performance metrics', which is exactly the subordination of society's demands to the body's wisdom.

items.value: Only conclusions 3 and 4 follow: the fine-tuning phase converges incomes as an exhausted technology is milked, and the technology sequence runs scavenging, hunting, farming, industrial
items.reasoning: In the breakaway phase the passage says follower per capita income is 'unchanged', which is not the same as progressing slowly, so 1 misstates it. Statement 2 supplies a mechanism the passage never gives: closing happens because 'the followers adopt the new technology', not because leaders stagnate, and the 'therefore' asserts a causation the text does not. Statement 3 tracks the fine-tuning description almost word for word. Statement 4 is true clause by clause given the dates (scavenging 3 MYA, hunting 1 MYA, farming 12 thousand years, industrial a little over 200 years). Runner-up is D (2, 3 and 4 only), which wins if 'leaders stagnate' is accepted as an implied consequence of convergence rather than an unsupported addition.

items.value: Only statement 3 is correct: technology leaders reach each new economic era first
items.reasoning: The model divides economic ERAS into three phases and economic ENTITIES into two categories, so statement 1's claim that it divides nations into three phases mixes the two divisions up. Statement 2 distorts the 'labour-productivity gap with the technology leader' into a gap 'between labour and productivity', which is a different thing entirely. Statement 4 adds the four figures (3,000,000 + 1,000,000 + 12,000 + 200 = 4,012,200) instead of taking the span, which runs from three million years ago to the present and is therefore three million years. Statement 3 follows because the leaders develop each new technology first and gain from it while the followers' income stays unchanged until they adopt it.

items.value: P and Q must be mixed in the ratio 1 : 3
items.reasoning: R must be half copper and half zinc, i.e. 50% copper. By alligation on copper the ratio of P to Q is (60 - 50) : (50 - 20) = 10 : 30 = 1 : 3. Checking directly with 1 kg of P and 3 kg of Q: copper is 0.2 + 1.8 = 2 kg and zinc is 0.8 + 1.2 = 2 kg out of 4 kg, which is the required equal split.

items.value: 9 such numbers A are possible: 41, 52, 63, 74, 85, 96, 71, 82 and 93
items.reasoning: Writing A = 10a + b and B = 10b + a gives A - B = 9(a - b), so for 27 to divide A - B the digit difference a - b must be a multiple of 3, that is 3, 6 or 9 since A is greater than B. The stem states that B is ALSO a two-digit number, which forces its tens digit b to be at least 1: a - b = 3 then gives 41, 52, 63, 74, 85 and 96; a - b = 6 gives 71, 82 and 93; and a - b = 9 needs b = 0 and is excluded. That is 9 numbers. Runner-up is C (12), which wins if the two-digit requirement on B is treated as loose description rather than a condition, since allowing a leading zero in B admits 30, 60 and 90 as well.

items.value: STOP is encoded as TSPO
items.reasoning: In ZERO to ADSN the shifts are Z to A (+1), E to D (-1), R to S (+1) and O to N (-1), so the code alternates one letter forward and one letter back across the four positions. Applying the same pattern to STOP gives S to T, T to S, O to P and P to O, that is TSPO. Option A (SPOT) and option D (POST) are mere rearrangements of the original letters and involve no shift at all, while option C (TSOP) breaks the alternation at the third letter.

Every tile is 3 feet wide and the strip is 3 feet wide, so the problem reduces to writing 100 as 3a + 7b + 11c. For n tiles the covered length is at least 3n, and each larger tile adds an excess of 4 feet (the 7-footer) or 8 feet (the 11-footer), so 100 - 3n must be a sum of 4s and 8s. n = 33 would need an excess of 1 and is impossible, while n = 32 needs 4, achieved by thirty-one 3-foot tiles and one 7-foot tile, so the maximum x is 32. For the minimum, 11n - 100 must likewise be a sum of 4s and 8s: n = 10 leaves 10 and n = 11 leaves 21, neither a multiple of 4, whereas n = 12 leaves 32 = 4 x 8, achieved by eight 11-foot tiles and four 3-foot tiles, so the minimum y is 12. Hence x - y = 20. (Requiring all three sizes to appear would give 28 - 12 = 16, which is not among the options, confirming that no such requirement is intended.)

items.value: The original speed was 200 km per hour
items.reasoning: 'Existing speed' means the speed the train has at the moment of the event, so the two reductions compound. In the actual run the train covers 200 km at v, then 400 km at v/2 after the accident, then the remaining 200 km at one-fourth of v/2, that is v/8, taking 200/v + 800/v + 1600/v = 2600/v. In the hypothetical run it covers 200 km at v, then 400 km at v/4, then 200 km at half of v/4, again v/8, taking 200/v + 1600/v + 1600/v = 3400/v. The difference 800/v equals 4 hours, giving v = 200, i.e. 13 hours against 17 hours. Runner-up is D (100), which wins if 'existing speed' is read as the ORIGINAL speed so that the two failures do not compound; that reading also yields exactly a 4-hour gap, at v = 100. The stem's separate and deliberate use of 'original' in its final question is what argues for the compounding reading.

A cut-off of 5.2 would select only two candidates and one of 5.0 would select four, whereas 5.1 selects exactly three, namely candidates 1, 3 and 2. Cut-offs of 5.3 and 5.4 select nobody at all.

items.value: Only relationship 3 holds: the absence of scientific consensus in S2 could be the reason for the alarmism-and-denial dynamic described in S3
items.reasoning: The three proposed relationships are not independent of one another. Relationship 1 asserts that S3 bears on S1 while relationship 2 asserts that S3 is unconnected to S1, so the two cannot both hold; and relationship 2 equally contradicts relationship 3, which asserts that S2 explains S3. Any option pairing 2 with either 1 or 3 is therefore self-contradictory, which rules out A, B and C and leaves '3 only'. On the substance this holds up: S3 does not deny S1's claim that protecting the environment is an existential necessity, it comments on the excesses of activism, so it is not a counterpoint to S1; and it is plainly connected to both statements, since it names climate change deniers, whose position feeds on precisely the missing consensus of S2. Runner-up is A (2 and 3 only), which wins if 'unconnected' is read narrowly as 'neither entails nor refutes' and so is treated as compatible with the merely speculative 'could be' of relationship 3.

items.value: A-1, B-4, C-3, D-2: captain and team informal and firm, judge and lawyers formal and firm, Vice Chancellor and Deputy Registrar formal and open-ended, peers and coworkers informal and open-ended
items.reasoning: A cricket captain is on familiar terms with his team yet his decisions on the field are final, which is informal and firm; peers and coworkers hold no authority over one another, so their exchange is informal and open-ended. Both remaining pairs are formal, and between them a courtroom is the most rule-bound setting on the list, with the judge's directions to counsel binding and not open to negotiation, so judge and lawyers is formal and firm. That leaves the Vice Chancellor and Deputy Registrar, administrative colleagues whose business is discussed, minuted and revisited, as formal and open-ended. Runner-up is A (A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2), which wins if 'firm' is taken to track line authority, since the Vice Chancellor is the Deputy Registrar's superior while an exchange of arguments in court is genuinely open until judgment; the whole item pivots on that one pair, as options A and B agree on the other three.

items.value: A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1: memorandum intimates a directive, flyer disseminates non-targeted information, Bcc informs confidentially, minutes record decisions
items.reasoning: Minutes are by definition the written record of what a meeting decided, so D pairs with 1. A flyer is posted or handed out to whoever happens to receive it, which is the very meaning of disseminating non-targeted information, so B pairs with 4. A blind carbon copy conceals a recipient from the other addressees, making it the confidential channel, so C pairs with 2. That leaves the memorandum, the standard office instrument for conveying an instruction or directive, paired with 3.

items.value: Only action 3 is appropriate: encourage personnel to seek each other's perspectives
items.reasoning: Directing staff to practise the cultural markers of other groups (1) is coercive and tokenistic, and imposing another community's practices on unwilling colleagues is more likely to deepen resentment than to resolve it. Allowing conflicts to 'resolve naturally over time' (2) is an abdication of managerial responsibility, and the precedent it sets is of absent leadership rather than appropriate leadership. Encouraging people to seek each other's perspectives (3) addresses the mutual misreading that drives cross-cultural friction and is the standard, non-coercive intervention.

items.value: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3: semantic is misunderstanding a word, cognitive is information overload, organisational is lack of feedback, affective is fear of social stigma
items.reasoning: Semantics is the study of meaning, so misunderstanding the meaning of a word is the semantic barrier, and 'affective' means emotional, which matches fear of social stigma; two of the four codes agree on both of these, so the item turns on the other pair. Information overload is a limit on the receiver's capacity to take in and process what is sent, which is a cognitive barrier, while an absent feedback loop is a defect in the organisation's own communication structure and channels, which is organisational. Runner-up is C (A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3), which wins if information overload is classed as a channel or organisational problem, as several textbooks do; against that, 'lack of feedback' is very hard to defend as a limitation of cognition.

items.value: Heads 1 and 2 only: size of family and budget
items.reasoning: A feasibility study for a family-oriented resort needs to know how large the visiting families are, since that drives room configuration and capacity, and what they are prepared to spend, since that drives pricing and viability. The number of earners in the family (3) is an intrusive proxy for income that budget already captures more directly and more reliably. Food allergies and dietary restrictions (4) are an operational detail relevant to catering for guests already booked, not evidence bearing on whether the resort should be built at all.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct: circular letters are usually addressed to a group of people
items.reasoning: A circular is by definition a single message sent to many recipients at once, so statement 1 is correct. Its content is standardised precisely because it goes to everybody in identical form, which makes statement 2, claiming non-standard and customised content, wrong. Appraisals and increments are individual and confidential matters conveyed by personal letters rather than by a document circulated to all staff, so statement 3 is wrong. And sending one identical letter to many people is cheaper per recipient than composing a separate letter for each, so statement 4 reverses the cost comparison.

items.value: C receives Rs 12,000 of the Rs 17,000 profit
items.reasoning: Take the total capital as K and the total duration as T. A contributes (K/3) x (T/3) = KT/9 and B contributes (K/4) x (T/4) = KT/16, while C's capital is K - K/3 - K/4 = 5K/12 held for the whole duration, contributing 5KT/12. Multiplying the ratio 1/9 : 1/16 : 5/12 by 144 gives 16 : 9 : 60, which sums to 85. C's share is therefore 17000 x 60/85 = 12,000, with A getting 3,200 and B 1,800, and the three add back to 17,000.

items.value: About 27 per cent, that is 2.71 litres of B in the 10-litre container
items.reasoning: The stem describes three replacements in all: the first litre of pure A removed, then one litre of the mixture, then the process performed 'once more'. Each replacement leaves nine-tenths of the chemical A that was present, so after three the quantity of A is 10 x (9/10) cubed = 7.29 litres and the quantity of B is 10 - 7.29 = 2.71 litres, which is 27.1 per cent and approximately 27. Two replacements would give 19 per cent and four would give about 34 per cent, neither of which appears among the options, which confirms that three is the intended count.

items.value: The question cannot be answered: distance is not determined by the number of deliveries, so no listed number of deliveries guarantees earnings above Rs 500
items.reasoning: Earnings are 5d + 2k, where d is the number of deliveries and k the kilometres covered, and nothing in the stem ties k to d. To 'definitely' meet the target the earnings must exceed 500 for every admissible distance, including a small one: 90 deliveries bring only Rs 450 from deliveries and would still need more than 25 km, 85 would need more than 37.5 km and 80 more than 50 km, none of which is guaranteed. The alternative reading, that he covers the full 100 km and so earns Rs 200 from distance, cannot be what is intended, because under it 80, 85 and 90 would all clear Rs 500 and three of the four options would be correct at once. Runner-up is A (80), the smallest listed number that could reach the target if the full 100 km were travelled, which wins only if 'definitely' is read as 'can'.
